body:
# Ninlil: canonical, contested, and the false forms on record

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Ninlil, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Ninlil to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **𒀭𒊩𒌆𒆤**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Ninlil**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: 'nin-LIL' — stress the second syllable and let the name end with a light, breathy lilt, like wind passing through reeds. The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *ninlil* differs from the canonical *Ninlil* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. The canonical form Ninlil is a baseline restoration: standard Assyriology writes the name without diacritics, and the canonical PuniCodex form preserves that plain spelling while asserting proper-name status.  In Akkadian and Assyrian sources Ninlil was identified with Mullissu (also spelled Mulliltu), the consort of the national god Aššur, whose cult rose with Assyrian empire.

And it never stopped working. Ninlil survives in Assyriological scholarship and in the modern recovery of Sumerian religion through ETCSL and the great lexical projects of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.  She is less famous in popular culture than her granddaughter Ištar or her consort Enlil, yet her role as wind-queen and mother of lunar and netherworld powers makes her essential to any coherent picture of the Mesopotamian pantheon.

## The Convention's Own History

Cuneiform writes a consonant inventory English does not have: š, ṣ, ṭ, ḫ mark sibilants and stops that Akkadian and Sumerian distinguished and meaning depends on — the difference between 'sun' and 'son' is exactly one ṣ. Assyriological transliteration (the sign lists of Borger and the Chicago Assyrian Dictionary) settled those marks over the last century and a half, and the register keeps them because dropping them merges gods, cities, and concepts that the tablets keep apart.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Ninlil** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Ninlil** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *ninlil* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Ninlil** stands at [/ninlil/](/ninlil/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 7 cited sources — ETCSL, Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia, Jacobsen, The Treasures of Darkness.
